outcome: Open in general as of 13 Oct 2026, and no source I opened claims a resolution of the general question. Since 26 Jan 2024 the events are: a July 2026 arXiv paper on overlapping unfoldings whose theorems do not decide the non-overlapping question; a March 2026 characterisation of band-unfolding for nested prismatoids that adds no new class; finite-instance counts from Shiota and co-authors (2024, 2025); and a GitHub repository created 8 Sep 2026 that claims a proof for all convex polytopes with at most six vertices, whose commits carry Claude Fable 5.1 co-author trailers, whose status is internally inconsistent, and which has had only a self-review.
problem_asks: The bullet asks one yes/no question, given in two equivalent forms: (a) does every convex polyhedron have a net, meaning a single non-overlapping planar polygon obtained by cutting the surface along edges of the polyhedron (a spanning tree of its edges); and (b) does every convex polyhedron have a simple edge-unfolding, the same notion under the bullet's second name. Unpacked: (1) the universal quantifier ranges over every convex polyhedron in three-dimensional Euclidean space; (2) for each such polyhedron, existence of at least one spanning tree of its edges whose cut yields a non-overlapping (simple) planar unfolding, so that 'some edge unfolding is non-overlapping' is what is asked, not 'every edge unfolding is non-overlapping'; (3) the bullet's alternative names (net, simple edge-unfolding, Dürer's conjecture, Dürer's unfolding problem) are treated as one question. Not asked: non-convex polyhedra, general (non-edge) unfoldings, or pseudo-edge unfoldings, although each is a neighbouring question.

events.what_happened: A. S. Tarasov, arXiv:0806.2360, 'Existence of a polyhedron which does not have a non-overlapping pseudo-edge unfolding'. The abstract says there exist a convex polyhedron P and a partition L of its surface into geodesic convex polygons such that no connected 'edge' unfolding of P without self-intersections exists whose spanning tree is a subset of the edge skeleton of L. The quotation marks around 'edge' in the abstract mark that the cuts follow the partition's skeleton, not the polyhedron's own edges.
events.revisions: v1 14 Jun 2008; v2 25 Sep 2008; v3 6 Oct 2008 (minor grammatical changes; current). No journal version found.
events.delivers: A non-overlapping unfolding fails for one pseudo-edge generalisation: a convex polyhedron with a partition into geodesic convex polygons, where the cuts must follow that partition's skeleton. This is a statement about the pseudo-edge version of the question; it does not show that some convex polyhedron lacks a non-overlapping unfolding along its actual edges.
events.remains: The actual-edge question for every convex polyhedron, which the abstract does not address.

checked_by.qualification: Authors of the Discrete & Computational Geometry paper on pseudo-edge unfoldings (research geometers)
checked_by.what_they_did: Per a search-result summary of their paper: they build a 340-vertex example that 'significantly simplifies an earlier construction by Tarasov'. The same summary says they distilled a negative result from Tarasov's preprint and describe it as 'highly original but flawed'. I did not confirm the 'flawed' wording in the text I opened, which is the abstract only.

events.doubts: A search-result summary attributes to Barvinok and Ghomi the description of Tarasov's preprint as 'highly original but flawed' (not verified in the paper text I opened). The abstract I read does not say how, or whether, the construction was repaired; the only public version is the 2008 preprint, and no journal version was found.
events.direction: Cuts against the pseudo-edge generalisation of Dürer's question (existence of a non-overlapping unfolding along a pseudo-edge skeleton). Silent on actual edges.
events.object: A convex polyhedron P with a partition of its surface into geodesic convex polygons, for which no connected non-self-intersecting unfolding exists along that partition's edge skeleton. The abstract gives no vertex count and no coordinates. Whether the construction is explicit or non-constructive is not established from the abstract; the later Barvinok–Ghomi proof rests on Pogorelov's existence theorem for convex caps.

events.what_happened: Mohammad Ghomi, 'Affine unfoldings of convex polyhedra', arXiv:1305.3231 (first posted 14 May 2013), published in Geometry & Topology 18 (2014), 3055–3090. Abstract: 'We show that every convex polyhedron admits a simple edge unfolding after an affine transformation.' The abstract says this leaves no combinatorial obstruction to a positive resolution of Dürer's unfoldability problem, and that it answers a question of Croft, Falconer and Guy.
events.revisions: v1 14 May 2013; v2 21 Apr 2014 (minor changes, index of notation; current).
events.delivers: For every convex polyhedron P there is an affine image of P that has a non-overlapping edge unfolding. The result is for the stretched shape only. It does not cover the polyhedron the problem asks about unless the affine map is the identity.
events.remains: Whether each convex polyhedron, unstretched, has a non-overlapping edge unfolding.

checked_by.qualification: Peer-reviewed research journal in geometry and topology
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted and published the paper, vol. 18 issue 5 (2014), pp. 3055–3090

checked_by.qualification: Named research mathematicians; authors of a preprint giving a short proof of Ghomi's result
checked_by.what_they_did: Reproved the affine-stretch existence result with a short proof, arXiv:1803.09828 (first posted 26 Mar 2018)

events.direction: Partial, toward a positive answer: it proves non-overlapping edge unfoldings exist after an affine stretch, and removes any purely combinatorial obstruction to the unstretched version.

events.what_happened: Joseph O'Rourke, 'Edge-Unfolding Nearly Flat Convex Caps', arXiv:1707.01006 (first posted 4 Jul 2017; v4 5 Jan 2021). Shows that a nearly flat, acutely triangulated convex cap can be cut along edges and laid out as a non-overlapping polygon, and that the closed polyhedron formed by adding the convex base under it can be edge-unfolded without overlap. The flatness needed depends on an acuteness gap alpha (about 5 degrees for alpha = 3 degrees, per the abstract). The arXiv page says v3 is the full version of a conference paper; the venue is named as SoCG 2018 only in a search summary.
events.revisions: v1 4 Jul 2017; v2 25 Aug 2017; v3 12 Mar 2018 (full version of a conference paper); v4 5 Jan 2021 (current).
events.delivers: A non-overlapping edge unfolding for one restricted class: nearly flat convex caps with acute triangulation, and the closed polyhedra built on them. It does not treat convex polyhedra in general.
events.remains: Every convex polyhedron outside the nearly flat acutely triangulated class, which is almost all of them.

checked_by.who: Referees of the conference version (venue SoCG 2018 per a search summary; not named on the arXiv page I opened)
checked_by.qualification: Peer review at a refereed computational geometry conference
checked_by.what_they_did: Refereed the conference version; the arXiv v3 comment states it is the full version of that paper

events.direction: Partial, toward a positive answer, for a restricted class.

events.what_happened: Nicholas Barvinok and Mohammad Ghomi, 'Pseudo-edge unfoldings of convex polyhedra', arXiv:1709.04944 (first posted 14 Sep 2017; v4 27 Feb 2019). Abstract: 'We construct a convex polyhedron K in Euclidean 3-space with a pseudo-edge graph with respect to which K is not unfoldable.' The example has 340 vertices, 'significantly simplifies an earlier construction by Tarasov', and 'confirms that Durer's conjecture does not hold for pseudo-edge unfoldings'. A pseudo-edge graph is a 3-connected graph in K whose vertices are those of K, whose edges are distance-minimising geodesics, and whose faces are convex. Published in Discrete & Computational Geometry (per a search summary; the Springer DOI was not opened).
events.revisions: v1 14 Sep 2017; v2 9 Nov 2017; v3 24 Jan 2019; v4 27 Feb 2019 (current).
events.delivers: A convex polyhedron with 340 vertices and a pseudo-edge graph with respect to which it is not unfoldable. It refutes the pseudo-edge generalisation of Dürer's conjecture only.
events.remains: The actual-edge version, for every convex polyhedron. The abstract does not address it.

checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted and published the paper, in the Ricky Pollack memorial issue (per a search summary: 2020, 64:671–689)

events.direction: Cuts against the pseudo-edge version of Dürer's conjecture (it is a counterexample to that generalisation). Silent on actual edges.
events.object: A convex polyhedron K with 340 vertices and a pseudo-edge graph with respect to which K is not unfoldable. The proof combines Pogorelov's theorem on convex caps with prescribed curvature (an existence result) and an unfoldability obstruction for almost flat convex caps due to Tarasov. The construction is therefore existence-based as far as the abstract shows; it is not given as explicit coordinates in the abstract.

events.what_happened: Hugo A. Akitaya, Erik D. Demaine, David Eppstein, Tomohiro Tachi and Ryuhei Uehara, 'Ununfoldable polyhedra with 6 vertices or 6 faces', Computational Geometry: Theory and Applications 103 (2022), article 101857 (DOI 10.1016/J.COMGEO.2021.101857). It began as a 2019 conference abstract, 'Minimal ununfoldable polyhedron' (JCDCGGG 2019). Per search-result summaries, which I could not verify because the full-text PDF did not decode: a topologically convex, non-convex polyhedron with 7 vertices and 6 faces that cannot be edge-unfolded; a companion example with 6 vertices and 7 faces; and the claim that every polyhedron with fewer than 6 vertices or fewer than 6 faces is edge-unfoldable.
events.revisions: Journal version CGTA 103 (2022) 101857; the Demaine listing marks the journal version as currently unavailable for download.
events.delivers: Edge-ununfoldable examples for topologically convex, non-convex polyhedra with 7 vertices and 6 faces (and with 6 vertices and 7 faces, per summary). For convex polytopes, the only relevant part would be the claim that fewer than 6 vertices or fewer than 6 faces forces edge-unfoldability; that claim is unverified here and, if true, leaves convex polytopes with exactly 6 vertices as the nearest open case.
events.remains: For convex polytopes: whether the fewer-than-6 claim covers convex polytopes at all (unverified), and the 6-vertex convex case.

checked_by.who: Computational Geometry: Theory and Applications (journal of record)

events.direction: Cuts against edge-unfoldability for topologically convex (non-convex) polyhedra. For convex polytopes it is at most a partial statement about very few vertices, and that is unverified.
events.object: A non-convex, topologically convex polyhedron with seven vertices and six faces that cannot be edge-unfolded, per the search summary's description: an apex, a base made of one triangle and one concave pentagon, and a side of triangles and concave quadrilaterals, mirror-symmetric. Its explicitness is not verified from the text.

events.what_happened: Erik D. Demaine, Martin L. Demaine and David Eppstein, 'Acutely Triangulated, Stacked, and Very Ununfoldable Polyhedra', arXiv:2007.14525 (first posted 28 Jul 2020). Constructs two families of polyhedra combinatorially equivalent to convex polyhedra, acutely triangulated and stacked, each 'very ununfoldable': any nonoverlapping multipiece edge unfolding has at least k pieces, for any chosen k. The paper describes them as topologically convex, not as convex polyhedra.
events.revisions: v1 28 Jul 2020; a CCCG 2020 version is listed on Demaine's site (not opened).
events.delivers: Polyhedra combinatorially equivalent to convex polyhedra that have no single-piece edge unfolding, in two families. Scope: topologically convex polyhedra, not convex ones. It does not decide the convex question.
events.remains: Convex polyhedra, which the paper's examples are not.
events.direction: Cuts against single-piece edge unfoldability only for topologically convex (non-convex) polyhedra. It is not a counterexample to the convex claim.
events.object: Two infinite families of polyhedra, acutely triangulated (every face an acute triangle) and stacked (tetrahedra glued face to face), each very ununfoldable. The construction details were not read, so whether they are explicit or non-constructive is not established.

events.what_happened: Manuel Radons, 'Edge-unfolding nested prismatoids', arXiv:2105.00555 (first posted 2 May 2021). Abstract: 'We show that every nested prismatoid has an edge-unfolding to a non-overlapping polygon in the plane.' A nested prismatoid is a prismatoid (convex hull of two convex polygons in parallel planes) whose top polygon's projection is properly contained in the base, or the reverse, per a search summary.
events.revisions: v1 2 May 2021; v2 5 Mar 2022; v3 21 Dec 2023 (current). No journal listed on the arXiv page.
events.delivers: A non-overlapping edge unfolding for every nested prismatoid, a restricted class of convex polyhedra. The non-nested prismatoids are not covered.
events.remains: Non-nested prismatoids (which O'Rourke's March 2026 paper lists as open), and every convex polyhedron outside the prismatoid class.

checked_by.qualification: Co-author of the prismatoid and band-unfolding papers; long-standing researcher on unfoldings
checked_by.what_they_did: Cites the result as having settled the nested case, in arXiv:2603.09813. This is citation, not an independent verification.

events.direction: Partial, toward a positive answer, for the nested-prismatoid class.

events.what_happened: Vincent Bian, Erik D. Demaine and Rachana Madhukara, 'Edge-Unfolding Prismatoids: Tall or Rectangular Base', arXiv:2106.14262 (first posted 27 Jun 2021; CCCG 2021, five pages). Shows a non-overlapping 'petal unfolding' of prismatoids in two cases: the top and base are sufficiently far apart; or the base is a rectangle and every other face is a nonobtuse triangle. Gives a counterexample showing the technique does not extend to a general quadrilateral base.
events.delivers: A non-overlapping edge unfolding for two sub-classes of prismatoids (far-apart top and base; rectangular base with nonobtuse triangular other faces).
events.remains: Prismatoids in general, and every convex polyhedron outside the prismatoid class.
events.direction: Partial, toward a positive answer, for two sub-classes of prismatoids.

events.what_happened: Joseph O'Rourke, 'Hamiltonian Quasigeodesics yield Nets', arXiv:2206.05353 (first posted 10 Jun 2022). Single-author note. It shows that every polyhedron with a Hamiltonian quasigeodesic (a simple closed quasigeodesic running along edges and visiting every vertex) can be edge-unfolded to a net, and that the class of such polyhedra is infinite. Later versions: v2 (21 Jun 2025) and v3 (24 Jun 2026). The v3 comment says the antiprism classes satisfy the main theorem but 'do not advance on Durer's problem'.
events.revisions: v1 10 Jun 2022; v2 21 Jun 2025; v3 24 Jun 2026 (current; adds antiprism classes, which the v3 comment says do not advance Dürer's problem).
events.delivers: A non-overlapping edge unfolding for every polyhedron with a Hamiltonian quasigeodesic, an infinite class. Restricted to polyhedra with that property.
events.remains: Polyhedra without a Hamiltonian quasigeodesic, which is the general problem.
events.direction: Partial, toward a positive answer, for the Hamiltonian-quasigeodesic class.

events.what_happened: Joseph O'Rourke, 'Polar Zonohedra Edge-Unfold to Nets', arXiv:2302.07747 (first posted 15 Feb 2023; v2 16 Feb 2023 adding a figure). Abstract: 'This note proves that every polar zonohedron has an edge-unfolding to a non-overlapping net.' Polar zonohedra are a continuous family with all faces rhombi of equal edge length, parameterised by the number of rhombi at each pole and a pole-angle parameter (per a search summary).
events.revisions: v1 15 Feb 2023; v2 16 Feb 2023 (added a figure).
events.delivers: A non-overlapping edge unfolding for every polar zonohedron, a continuous family. Restricted class.
events.direction: Partial, toward a positive answer, for a restricted class.

events.what_happened: Takumi Shiota and Toshiki Saitoh, 'Overlapping Edge Unfoldings for Archimedean Solids and (Anti)prisms' (WALCOM 2023; Springer chapter DOI 10.1007/978-3-031-27051-2_4, per a search result), and its journal version 'Overlapping edge unfoldings for convex regular-faced polyhedra', Theoretical Computer Science 1002 (2024), article 114593 (per a search summary). Per the chapter summary: they propose 'rotational unfolding' to find overlapping edge unfoldings; all edge unfoldings of an icosidodecahedron, a rhombitruncated cuboctahedron and of Archimedean prisms and antiprisms with 3≤n≤23 and 3≤m≤11 do not overlap; n-gonal prisms (n≥24), m-gonal antiprisms (m≥12) and a snub cube do have overlapping edge unfoldings.
events.revisions: Journal version TCS 1002 (2024), article 114593 (per search summary).
events.delivers: For finitely many named polyhedra and bounded size ranges: every edge unfolding is non-overlapping (positive instances). For larger prisms, antiprisms and the snub cube: overlapping edge unfoldings exist. Finite instances of a universal claim; they settle nothing about the universal claim either way.
events.remains: Every convex polyhedron outside the listed finite families and ranges.

checked_by.who: WALCOM 2023 programme committee and Springer (refereed conference proceedings, per the chapter's citation)
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted the paper for publication in the proceedings (the chapter was not opened)

events.direction: Both ways for finite families: positive (non-overlap for listed small cases) and negative (overlap for large prisms, antiprisms and the snub cube). Neither bears on the universal claim.
events.object: Explicit overlapping edge unfoldings for n-gonal Archimedean prisms (n≥24), m-gonal Archimedean antiprisms (m≥12), and three types of overlapping edge unfoldings of a snub cube with two vertices in contact, all found by computer enumeration with 'rotational unfolding' (not AI).

events.what_happened: Takumi Shiota, Yudai Enomoto, Takashi Horiyama and Toshiki Saitoh, 'The Number of Non-overlapping Edge Unfoldings in Convex Regular-faced Polyhedra', EuroCG 2024, Ioannina, Greece, 13–15 March 2024. Uses zero-suppressed binary decision diagrams to enumerate and count non-overlapping edge unfoldings of named regular-faced polyhedra (three Archimedean solids and twenty Johnson solids, plus Archimedean prisms and antiprisms in bounded ranges, per a search summary). The paper PDF did not decode; the claims are from the abstract, slides and summaries.
events.revisions: Expanded in the CCCG 2025 paper (next event).
events.delivers: Exact counts of non-overlapping edge unfoldings for a finite list of named polyhedra; each count is positive for those polyhedra. Finitely many instances of a universal claim, so nothing settles the universal question.
events.remains: Every other convex polyhedron, and the universal claim.

checked_by.qualification: Peer review at a refereed conference
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted the paper for EuroCG 2024; the conference site confirms the dates

events.direction: Positive instances only: non-overlapping edge unfoldings counted for finitely many named polyhedra.

events.what_happened: Joseph O'Rourke, 'Every Combinatorial Polyhedron Can Unfold with Overlap', Computing in Geometry and Topology 4(2) (2025), articles 2:1–2:19, DOI 10.57717/cgt.v4i2.54, published 11 May 2025. It answers, in the negative, a question of Malkevitch: is there a combinatorial polyhedron for which every realization and every spanning cut-tree gives a net? Its answer: every combinatorial polyhedron has some realization and some cut-tree whose edge-unfolding overlaps.
events.revisions: Journal publication 11 May 2025. The arXiv posting date was not found; a search summary mentions an O'Rourke result from 2019 that I did not verify, so the first public version may predate 2024.
events.delivers: Overlap is unavoidable for some realization and some cut-tree of every combinatorial type. This is a statement about existence of one overlapping unfolding for a realization, and it does not refute the claim that each convex polyhedron has some non-overlapping unfolding. The realization in question may be non-convex.
events.remains: The problem as stated: for each convex polyhedron, a non-overlapping edge unfolding.

checked_by.who: Computing in Geometry and Topology (journal of record)
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted and published the paper, vol. 4 issue 2 (2025)

events.time_since_posted: about 1 year 5 months since journal publication
events.direction: Orthogonal: about overlapping unfoldings, answering a combinatorial question in the negative. It does not decide the convex non-overlap claim.

events.what_happened: Takumi Shiota, Yudai Enomoto, Masashi Gorobe, Takashi Horiyama, Tonan Kamata, Toshiki Saitoh and Ryuhei Uehara, 'The Number of Non-overlapping Unfoldings in Convex Polyhedra', CCCG 2025, Toronto, 13–15 August 2025. A zero-suppressed-BDD algorithm counts non-overlapping edge unfoldings by removing minimal overlapping patterns, for edge and lattice unfoldings, with experiments on several convex polyhedra (per search-result summaries; the PDF was not opened).
events.delivers: A counting method and counts for listed convex polyhedra. These are finitely many instances, and nothing in the paper, as summarised, extends to the universal claim.
events.remains: Every convex polyhedron not in the experimental list, and the universal claim.

checked_by.qualification: Peer review at a refereed conference

events.direction: Positive instances only: non-overlapping edge unfoldings counted for listed convex polyhedra.

events.what_happened: Joseph O'Rourke, 'Prismatoid Band-Unfolding Revisited', arXiv:2603.09813 (first posted 10 Mar 2026; v2 23 Mar 2026; v3 18 Sep 2026, current). It characterises when band-unfolding a nested prismatoid is non-overlapping (a radially monotone top polygon and a 'safe cut' on the band), and shows the known band-unfolding counterexample (O'Rourke 2007, arXiv:0710.0811) is essentially the only kind of counterexample of its type. The paper states that the result does not expand the known class of shapes with an edge-unfolding, and that 'It remains unknown if every prismatoid has a nonoverlapping edge-unfolding.'
events.revisions: v1 10 Mar 2026; v2 23 Mar 2026; v3 18 Sep 2026 (current). The abstract and body cite the 2007 counterexample under different labels (search summary).
events.delivers: A characterisation of when band-unfolding works for nested prismatoids, a class already settled by Radons (2021). It adds no new class of shapes and covers no non-nested case.
events.remains: Non-nested prismatoids, which the paper says remain open, and every convex polyhedron outside the prismatoid class.
events.direction: Neither for nor against. It reaffirms that the general question is open. The counterexample it discusses is to the band-unfolding method, not to the existence of an edge-unfolding.

events.what_happened: Hugo A. Akitaya, Erik D. Demaine, Fabian Frei, Stefan Langerman, Anna Lubiw and Joseph O'Rourke, 'Overlapping Unfoldings of Cones and Convex Polyhedra', arXiv:2607.09606 (cs.CG; submitted 10 Jul 2026; v1 only at my fetch), prepared for CCCG 2026 (Orillia, 12–14 Aug 2026, per a venue listing). Theorem 1.1 (as rendered): there is a convex polyhedron P such that, for any t, P can be unfolded using general cuts to have overlap thickness t. Theorem 1.4 (as rendered): for any t there is a convex polyhedron with an edge unfolding achieving overlap thickness at least t. The introduction says the Platonic solids have only non-overlapping edge unfoldings, and that every convex polyhedron has a non-overlapping general (source or star) unfolding. The paper says Dürer's problem 'has remained unsolved'. The first page carries the author-block footnote 'Artificial first author to highlight that the other authors (in alphabetical order) worked as an equal group', attached to the group label 'MIT CompGeom Group'. This is a placeholder for authorship, and it names no AI system.
events.revisions: v1 10 Jul 2026 only, as of my fetch.
events.delivers: Existence, for each thickness t, of a convex polyhedron having at least one edge unfolding with overlap thickness at least t; and existence of a convex polyhedron with general-cut unfoldings of any overlap thickness. Concerns overlapping unfoldings. It does not establish that any given convex polyhedron lacks a non-overlapping edge unfolding, and it does not decide the problem's existence claim.
events.remains: Whether every convex polyhedron has a non-overlapping edge unfolding (the problem as stated). Untouched.
events.direction: Orthogonal to the problem. Its theorems are existence statements about overlapping unfoldings, which are consistent with a polyhedron also having a non-overlapping edge unfolding. Its gadget P1 (stated as six vertices, achieving overlap thickness 2) is relevant to the six-vertex claim in the next-but-one event, and whether P1 is convex, and which unfolding attains thickness 2, are not established from the text I read.
events.object: Explicit constructions from cone gadgets: a cone with apex curvature (a/b)·2π has a cut path achieving overlap thickness b−a (Lemma 1.2); a cone with apex curvature an irrational multiple of π achieves any overlap thickness (Lemma 1.3). Gadget P1 has n = 6 vertices and achieves t = 2; gadget P2 has n = 10 and achieves t = 3, per the text as rendered. These are constructions, not existence-only arguments.

events.what_happened: ProofAtlas (proofatlas.ai), 'Collaboration' page for 'Dürer's Edge-Unfolding Conjecture'. The page says it was status-checked 2 Aug 2026 and source-recorded 6 Aug 2026. It describes a 'retained sixth-pass packet' that closes 'coordinate-uniform octahedral coverage and therefore every triangular reciprocal type with at most three interior vertices', and reports eight of sixteen four-interior types covered by 'leaf refinements' (labelled 'source-reported', 'dependencies incomplete'). It reports a 26-vertex construction as 'eliminated' and some computations as 'reported unreproduced' because the generating script is absent. The page says the packet 'leaves Dürer's full edge-unfolding conjecture open' and calls the remaining types 'not counterexamples'. It labels the research question 'not proof evidence'.
events.revisions: The packet is undated. Page stamps: status checked 2 Aug 2026; context collected 2 Aug 2026; source recorded 6 Aug 2026; next context review 2 Nov 2026. The first public date may be earlier than the status stamp.
events.delivers: Claimed partial coverage of named sub-classes: triangular reciprocal types with at most three interior vertices, and eight of sixteen four-interior types. The text I read does not define these classes in full. The page says explicitly that the full conjecture is not settled.
events.remains: The full conjecture; by the page's own account, eight four-interior types are unresolved, as are all types outside the named classes.
events.time_since_posted: about 2 months since the status check
events.directly_checkable: The page mentions an 'embedded deterministic verifier' for a census of five maximal planar graphs and sixteen types. No artefact is linked on the page I read.
events.doubts: The packet is undated and unattributed; no paper or arXiv posting is linked. The page itself labels the research question 'not proof evidence'. Some computations are 'reported unreproduced' with the generating script missing, and some dependencies are 'incomplete'. The platform calls itself 'AI-first' and offers users 'model runs' and 'hosted agent' runs, but the page does not say who or what produced this packet.
events.direction: Partial, toward a positive answer, for the named sub-classes. Its claim that the remaining types 'are not counterexamples' is an assertion on the page, not a proof.

events.what_happened: GitHub repository slef/EdgeUnfoldings, described as 'Dürer's problem for convex polytopes with at most six vertices: proof status, notes, experiments'. Created 8 Sep 2026 (first visible commit 7 Sep 2026 23:27 UTC; last visible commit 12 Sep 2026 00:59 UTC). The README calls it a 'working repository for a human-readable proof that every convex polytope with at most six vertices has a non-overlapping edge unfolding, in the style of J. DiBiase's 1990 thesis'. HANDOFF.md states, in its top entry (12 Sep 2026): 'All seven six-vertex type arguments are now written, pending independent mathematical review.' An 11 Sep entry says: 'The full n=6 case remains unproved', and a later section says 'the full n=6 theorem is not claimed'; the audit itself calls the status 'conflicting'. The 12 Sep self-review file (n6/PROOF_REVIEW_20260912.md) says: 'No mathematical gap was identified in this self-review' and 'This is not an independent audit or formal verification.' The commits are authored under the name Stefan Langerman. The 2026 Akitaya et al. paper gives Langerman a slef.org address in its author footnote, the same handle as the GitHub account. The repository owner's profile lists no affiliation.
events.revisions: Repository created 8 Sep 2026; commits run to 12 Sep 2026; README and audit both say independent review is still needed. No later state checked.
events.delivers: If the proofs stand: every convex polytope with at most six vertices has a non-overlapping edge unfolding. That covers combinatorial types with at most six vertices, not seven or more. The repository's own tally (Lemma A settles n=4, n=5 and three six-vertex types; the audit lists seven six-vertex types as written) is not consistent across its entries, and its status is unreviewed.
events.remains: Convex polytopes with seven or more vertices (the audit says n=7 was not started as of 8 Sep). It also lists items that may or may not be premises of the six-vertex proof: the fixed two-tree minus-edge conjecture (listed as open), the every-slit Lemma F and Triple Lemma under H alone (listed as stronger open questions, with only selected-slit versions proved), and nonsimplicial six-vertex types with maximum curvature at least π (listed as open on 11 Sep). Whether these are premises is not stated clearly.

checked_by.who: The repository's own self-review (n6/PROOF_REVIEW_20260912.md, dated 12 Sep 2026)
checked_by.qualification: Written inside the repository, by its team; the file names no reviewer. Whether any part was drafted by an AI system is not stated.
checked_by.what_they_did: Self-review reporting no mathematical gap; the file states it is not an independent audit and that 'independent mathematical review and formal verification remain outstanding'

events.directly_checkable: Explicit cases can be checked by hand from the written proofs (the octahedron-minus-edge graph, the prism with one diagonal, the Lemma A cases). The status page (durer_small_n/notes/status.html, deployed to GitHub Pages) shows the nets of the seven six-vertex types and an interactive octahedron widget. The repository's test suite (300 passing, per the review) checks finite and algebraic claims only.
events.doubts: (a) Internal inconsistency: the top HANDOFF entry says all seven six-vertex types are written pending review, while an 11 Sep entry says 'The full n=6 case remains unproved' and a later section says 'the full n=6 theorem is not claimed'. The audit calls the status 'conflicting'. (b) Open items recorded in the 12 Sep review: 'Neither five-tree minimality nor sufficiency of the four cofacial trees alone has been proved'; 'Lemma F and the Triple Lemma under H alone (arbitrary slits) remain stronger open questions'; 'The fixed two-tree minus-edge conjecture is unchanged and open'; 'The unranked octahedron shortcut is unproved'; 'The minus-edge transfer of the face-cap rule is open'. (c) The prism was listed as open in the 11 Sep entries, before a 12 Sep prism proof. (d) Lemma L: on one day one entry says 'Lemma L is proved' and another 'General L remains open (0/3 universal obligations)'. (e) Earlier reductions were refuted and retired: the far-fan reduction and the unrestricted fan-to-petal reduction. (f) Several Lemma F results are described as 'numerically established, not proved'. The review says 'No numerical experiment is a universal-proof premise', and an SMT query returned unknown/timeout. (g) Only self-review; independent review is explicitly outstanding. (h) The repository's claim for n≤5 may depend on the Akitaya et al. fewer-than-6 result, which I could not verify.
events.direction: Toward a positive answer for convex polytopes with at most six vertices, if the proofs stand. It is a claimed resolution of a restricted case, not of the general question.

systems.what_it_did: Per the repository's own records. Commits carry 'Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>' trailers. Examples: commit 1b309011 (7 Sep 2026, 23:28 UTC): 'Lemma F session 2026-09-08: octa.py module, overlap classification, rotation-picture argument, adversarial tests, LaTeX notes, handoff update'; commit 1165d5d1 (7 Sep 2026, 23:36 UTC): 'Read DiBiase 1990 thesis: summary in notes/dibiase_summary.md, handoff corrected (simplicial only, safe-spot lemmas)'. HANDOFF.md says the account 'preserves Claude's prior work and chronology', but it does not itemise which proof steps the model produced. The trailers appear on the 7–8 Sep commits I could read; the 9–12 Sep commits I could read show none, though the commit list was truncated. The trailer is written by the committer, so it is the repository's own account of co-authorship. Whether the rotation-picture argument, or any step the six-vertex proofs depend on, is load-bearing AI output is not settled by the sources.

disputes.summary: Unverified attribution: one search-result summary says the 'Dürer's conjecture' label 'appears to have been first published by Grünbaum'. No source I opened supports this. The ProofAtlas page and the TOPP entry credit Shephard (1975) as the origin of the question, and the Dürer link is to the 1525 drawings. Recorded here so the later pass can check it.

summary: Shephard's 1975 question, also called Dürer's problem, is still open on every source I opened from 2025 and 2026. The Wikipedia article 'Net (polyhedron)' says it 'remains unanswered'. TOPP Problem 9 lists it as Open and says it is 'a widespread hunch that the answer is yes'. Demaine and O'Rourke's 2025 book update says it remains open as of writing (dated Aug–Sep 2025 by search summaries; the PDFs did not decode, so that is unverified). O'Rourke's March 2026 paper says 'It remains unknown if every prismatoid has a nonoverlapping edge-unfolding'. Akitaya et al. (July 2026) say it 'has remained unsolved'. Since 26 January 2024 the events are: (i) the July 2026 arXiv paper on overlapping unfoldings (Akitaya, Demaine, Frei, Langerman, Lubiw, O'Rourke), whose theorems give convex polyhedra with overlapping edge unfoldings of any thickness; this is existence of overlapping unfoldings and does not decide existence of a non-overlapping one; (ii) O'Rourke's March 2026 band-unfolding characterisation for nested prismatoids, which adds no class; (iii) Shiota and co-authors' 2024 and 2025 counts of non-overlapping edge unfoldings for finitely many named polyhedra, which are finite instances and settle nothing universal; and (iv) the repository slef/EdgeUnfoldings, created 8 Sep 2026, which claims a human-readable proof that every convex polytope with at most six vertices has a non-overlapping edge unfolding. Event (iv) is the only claimed resolution of any class I found, so it carries most of the weight. Its AI involvement is stated in its own records: commits carry 'Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1' trailers, and HANDOFF.md says its account 'preserves Claude's prior work and chronology'. No source I opened says which proof steps the model produced. Its own status is inconsistent (the top HANDOFF entry says all seven six-vertex types are written pending review; an 11 Sep entry says 'The full n=6 case remains unproved'), its only review is a self-review that says it is not an audit, and the commits are under Stefan Langerman, who is also a co-author of event (i); the paper's footnote gives Langerman a slef.org address that matches the GitHub handle. Five close calls for the later pass. (a) The 'Artificial first author' footnote on event (i) labels the group 'MIT CompGeom Group' and says it stands for an equal-authorship convention. It is not an AI system, and I have recorded it as none found. (b) The ProofAtlas packet (event proofatlas-2026-sixth-pass-packet) reports partial coverage of named types with no named producer, on a platform that calls itself 'AI-first'. (c) The repository's review file mentions a branch named 'codex/proof-review-tidy'. That names a tool only as a branch label, and no source says what it did, so I have not listed it as a system. (d) The six-vertex claim and Akitaya et al.'s fewer-than-six result (which I could not read in full) may or may not overlap in scope for convex polytopes with five or fewer vertices. (e) Wikipedia's 'Shephard's problem' article is about a different question (projection volumes of centrally symmetric convex bodies, Petty–Schneider), found by search and not opened; the unfolding question is covered in 'Net (polyhedron)', which I did open. Searches for AI results on this problem from labs and announcements (OpenAI, Google DeepMind's AlphaProof/AlphaEvolve/Gemini Deep Think, Anthropic) found nothing except the repository. The AI-maths headlines I found in 2026 concern other problems (an Erdős unit-distance result, reported in search summaries).
competing_reading: Reading (1): the repository is a claimed resolution for convex polytopes with at most six vertices, pending review, and should move this problem to 'partially settled, restricted to ≤6 vertices' once its proofs are checked. Reading (2): it is an unreviewed working document whose own top entry and its 11 Sep entry contradict each other, whose review is a self-review, and whose listed open items may be premises; on that reading no event so far settles any class and the problem stays open with nothing counted. On AI: the co-author trailers and the phrase 'preserves Claude's prior work' can be read as tooling assistance (code, notes, proofreading, handoff writing) rather than load-bearing mathematics; the rotation-picture argument and the proof steps are the candidates for load-bearing output, and the sources do not say which steps the model produced. A third reading of event (i) would count the 'Artificial first author' footnote as an AI authorship claim; I think the footnote is an authorship convention, since it describes an equal group, and I have not treated it as AI involvement.
what_would_settle_it: (1) Independent written verification of the six-vertex proofs (an arXiv posting, a journal submission, or a named expert's digest), and a repository state without the conflicting entries. (2) The repository owner's explicit statement of which listed open items (the fixed two-tree minus-edge conjecture; Lemma F and the Triple Lemma under H alone; nonsimplicial six-vertex types with curvature at least π; the prism's minimality) are or are not premises of the six-vertex proof. (3) The full text of Akitaya, Demaine, Eppstein, Tachi and Uehara (CGTA 2022), to check whether the fewer-than-six claim covers convex polytopes and so what the six-vertex case would add. (4) The full text of arXiv:2607.09606: whether gadget P1 (six vertices, overlap thickness 2) is convex, and which edge unfolding attains thickness 2; if P1 is a convex polytope with six vertices, the repository's six-vertex claim would need to exhibit a non-overlapping unfolding for it. (5) A written statement, from the authors or in the repository, of which steps in the six-vertex proofs were produced by Claude Fable 5.1 and which were written or checked by people, and whether the 'Co-Authored-By' trailers denote drafting, code, or mathematics. (6) The Demaine–O'Rourke Chapter 22 PDFs (22.1, 22.4, 22.5) for their dates and open-problem lists. (7) A citing paper or a repository-linked preprint for the six-vertex result, or the absence of one a year on.

incomplete: Several sources could not be read as text, so the relevant claims rest on search-result summaries and are flagged as unverified where they matter: the JCDCGGG 2019 Akitaya et al. paper (the fewer-than-six theorem is unverified), the EuroCG 2024 and CCCG 2025 Shiota papers (abstracts and summaries only), the GFALOP update PDFs 22.1 and 22.5 (dates conflict across summaries: Aug 25, Aug 28, Sep 3 2025), and the PDF of arXiv:2607.09606 (I used its HTML rendering; theorem statements are as rendered). The Shiota–Saitoh Springer chapter, the Discrete & Computational Geometry publication of Barvinok–Ghomi, the Geometry & Topology publication of Ghomi, and the SoCG/CCCG venue details for O'Rourke's 2017 paper were not opened directly. For the GitHub repository I read the README, HANDOFF.md, the 12 Sep self-review, the first 100 commit entries (truncated; the full history was not read, and the commits after 12 Sep were not checked), the repository metadata and the owner profile. I did not read the full proof texts (n6/ and durer_small_n/ notes), so I cannot say which proof steps depend on which open items beyond the audit's own list. The link between the GitHub handle slef and co-author Stefan Langerman rests on the slef.org address in the arXiv footnote and the commit author name; I have not verified control of slef.org beyond that. I did not find the origin of the 'Dürer's conjecture' label beyond Shephard (1975), and the Grünbaum attribution in one search summary is unverified. The 'Co-Authored-By' trailers were visible only on the commits in the fetched part of the list, so the AI attribution for commits after 8 Sep is incomplete. No funding, cost or token figures were disclosed.
